explanation: In Vietnam, dining is fairly casual and hosts often pour for guests as a gesture of hospitality, so pouring your own drink is not inherently rude. However, at shared or ceremonial drinking — especially rice wine from a communal cup — the eldest is served first and the cup is refilled for the next person, so grabbing or self-pouring in that setting can seem impolite. Foreigners are usually given leeway, but offering to pour for others before yourself is the safer habit.
local_tip: At a shared table, pour for the eldest and others first and let someone pour for you; only pour your own if no one is serving and the meal is casual.

also_check.note: Pouring for others is expected; filling your own glass is seen as slightly self-serving.
Similar to Japan — pour for elders and receive from others rather than self-pouring.
Toasting customs favor pouring for others, but self-pouring at casual meals is common and accepted.

sources.title: Asian Food Etiquette – How to Eat, Drink and Dine Like the Locals
